clips.title: HashiCorp Packer Tutorial: Building Custom Images for AWS, Azure, and Docker
clips.why: Why bake at all: mutable and immutable infrastructure, custom images, and the workflow Packer automates.
look: Immutable: instead of changing running machines, you build a new image and replace the machines.
A custom image already holds everything a machine needs when it starts.
The steps Packer automates: start a machine, change it, save it as an image.
clips.after: Our sandbox VMs are immutable in this sense: every run gets a fresh VM from the promoted image, and the image is rebuilt every night.

clips.title: Ansible Desired State Configuration & Idempotency Explained
clips.why: A three-minute conversation that explains desired state and idempotency in Ansible, the idea behind changed=0.
look: Desired state: you describe what the machine should look like.
Idempotency: running the same thing again changes nothing if the state is already right.
Why that makes automation safe to run again.
clips.after: Our image role must give changed=0 on a second run; a task that repeats an action, such as appending a line, breaks that.

clips.title: Ansible in 100 Seconds
clips.why: A fast overview of the Ansible words you meet in the lab: inventory, playbooks, tasks and modules.
look: The inventory: which machines Ansible works on.
A playbook is YAML with tasks, and each task calls a module.
Ansible needs no agent program on the machine: it connects to it and runs the tasks.
clips.after: In the lab the machine is a container and Ansible connects with docker exec; in our Packer build it is the temporary EC2 VM.

practice.q: Put one night of the sandbox image in order.
items: Packer starts a temporary VM from the base image
Ansible runs the image role on it
Packer saves the disk as an AMI on the testing channel and deletes the VM
A smoke test boots one VM from the new AMI and runs the checks
The workflow copies ami-id to ami-id-previous and writes the new AMI into ami-id
practice.why: Nothing reaches the runs until the smoke test passes, and the old pointer is saved before the new one is written, so rollback is always possible.

options.why: The second run fails, because the user already exists, or you need extra shell logic to guard it.
The user module describes a state. On the second run it finds the user and reports ok.
Every run appends the line again, so the file grows, and a typo here can lock everyone out of sudo.

practice.q: The launch templates never name an AMI. Finish the line so every new VM reads the promoted image.
practice.hint: The SSM parameter that the promote step writes.
practice.why: AWS reads the parameter each time a VM starts, so promoting or rolling back an image changes no HCL and needs no apply.

practice.q: Why does the nightly build start from the base image instead of from yesterday's sandbox image?

options.text: Because Packer cannot start from an image it built itself.
options.why: It could. The reason is about what goes into the image.

options.text: So the image is exactly what the recipe says; leftovers and mistakes from earlier builds cannot pile up.
options.why: Starting from a clean base each time means the role is the whole truth about the image.

options.text: Because yesterday's image has already expired.
options.why: Only testing images expire. Yesterday's release image is still there, and it is the rollback target.

practice.q: Fill in the recap of a healthy second run of the same playbook on the same machine.
practice.hint: What should an idempotent playbook change the second time?
practice.why: Every task finds its state already true, so nothing changes. Any other number points at a task that repeats an action.
